A: That limit would appear to apply to the total size of the instance, but you probably don't need to worry about that too much unless you are seeing any performance issues. texts.full_text: identifying the glioma grade and molecular subtype is very helpful. However, the traditional way to identify the glioma grade and molecular subtype is to acquire tumor tissue by surgery or biopsy, which causes significant trauma to the human body. The disadvantages of conventional invasive methods motivate us to develop a reliable method for predicting glioma grade and survival. Recently, mounting evidence has suggested that preoperative hematological markers related to nutrition, coagulation, and inflammation are predictive and prognostic factors of cancers (Perisanidis et al., [@B16]; He J. et al., [@B5]; Hwang et al., [@B7]; Ye et al., [@B24]; Zhao et al., [@B26]). In gliomas, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) (Han et al., [@B4]; Lopes et al., [@B10]), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) (Han et al., [@B4](Li et al., [@B9]), and lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) (Wang et al., [@B22]) have been identified as potential biomarkers for predicting tumor grade, prognosis, and response to therapy. These hematological markers are derived from routine blood tests, making them minimally invasive options compared to surgical biopsies. The NLR is calculated by dividing the absolute neutrophil count by the absolute lymphocyte count in peripheral blood. An elevated NLR has been associated with a poor prognosis in various cancers, including gliomas (Han et al., [@B4]). Similarly, PLR and LMR are derived from platelet and monocyte counts relative to lymphocytes, respectively. These ratios reflect systemic inflammation and immune response status, which can influence tumor progression and patient outcomes. Recent studies have shown that these hematological markers not only correlate with glioma grade but also provide valuable prognostic information regarding overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). For instance, a higher NLR or PLR has been linked to more aggressive tumor behavior and shorter survival times in patients with high-grade gliomas

texts.full_text: Use of multiple fins with an unmerged epitaxial source region and an unmerged epitaxial drain region (hereinafter collectively referred to as “unmerged epitaxial source/drain regions) enables further tailoring of device specification and increased performed. However, with unmerged epitaxial source/drain regions, there is significant loss of contact area since the source contact and the drain contact (hereinafter collectively referred to as source/drain contacts) are typically formed over top portions of the epitaxial source/drain regions and most of the epitaxial source/drain regions are covered by an interlayer dielectric layer. This results in a reduced contact area, which in turn increases the contact resistance and can degrade the overall performance of the device. To address this issue, the present application discloses a novel source contact structure and a drain contact structure that are designed to maximize the contact area with the unmerged epitaxial source/drain regions, thereby reducing contact resistance and improving device performance. In one embodiment, the source contact structure and the drain contact structure are formed by etching a recess into the interlayer dielectric layer to expose a portion of the unmerged epitaxial source/drain regions. The recess is then filled with a conductive material, such as tungsten or cobalt, to form the source and drain contacts. The recess is designed to have a shape and depth that optimizes the contact area with the unmerged epitaxial source/drain regions while minimizing the risk of shorting between the source and drain contacts. In another embodiment, the source and drain contacts are formed by a self-aligned process, where the contacts are aligned to the edges of the unmerged epitaxial source/drain regions, thereby ensuring a consistent and reliable contact area. This self-aligned process can be achieved by using a hard mask or a spacer to define the contact openings, which are then filled with the conductive material. The disclosed source contact structure and drain contact structure

texts.full_text: e bike. It took several weeks of that and he got it and has been happily biking since. I have at least once or twice referred to that process as the worst part of parenting because of the amazingly awful pain of running while squatting and holding up a bike with a biker who’s going at good speed. It’s seriously not a good time, though of course worth it for the fun of the kid being able to ride. Lilah has been riding on training wheels for years and last summer I thought she was ready to ride without them and we tried a few times the same way but it was hard and scary and neither of us were very motivated to keep going. The weather has just turned the corner on warm enough here to want to be out and so I decided to ask if she’d like to try a different approach that my sister who is practically on a bike most of the time suggested. Lilah kept her feet off the pedals and just pushed along and balanced. She was comfortable with it because she could stop whenever and go as slow or fast as she wanted. It was tough going up hills and not very practical at first even on flat ground but she really started practicing going down a gentle hill at the park by us. Today she begged to go “balance biking” and so we all went and halfway through she started putting her feet on the pedals and going! She’s so proud and I’m so excited about bike trips together and I’m thrilled that we figured out a less scary way for her to get the hang of it! Woohoo! Biking and picnics here we come! texts.full_text: ly ill patients. Distributive shock is a common problem in intensive care. Systemic hypotension is a medical emergency and will cause end-organ injury if not reversed. There are relatively few medications available to treat distributive shock. Catecholamines are most widely used for this indication and work by stimulating alpha- and/or beta-adrenergic receptors. Vasopressin and corticosteroids may have a role in reversing refractory shock and work primary through nonadrenergic mechanisms. In critically ill patients, the use of vasopressor agents like vasopressin and catecholamines can be crucial in managing distributive shock, a condition characterized by systemic hypotension and poor tissue perfusion. Distributive shock, which can result from various causes such as sepsis, anaphylaxis, or neurogenic shock, requires prompt recognition and intervention to prevent organ damage and mortality. Catecholamines, including norepinephrine and dopamine, are commonly employed in the treatment of distributive shock due to their ability to increase systemic vascular resistance and improve cardiac output. These agents exert their effects by activating alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors on the walls of blood vessels and the heart, respectively. While norepinephrine is more selective for alpha-receptors, dopamine has a broader spectrum of action, affecting both alpha- and beta-receptors, as well as the dopamine D1 and D2 receptors. Vasopressin, on the other hand, is a hormone that acts primarily through the V1a receptors found on vascular smooth muscle cells. It constricts blood vessels and increases blood pressure by enhancing the effects of norepinephrine on the vasculature. Vasopressin may also have a role in reducing fluid loss through its action on the kidneys, thereby helping to maintain intravascular volume. Corticosteroids, such as hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone, can also be considered in the treatment of distributive shock, particularly in cases where shock is refractory to conventional vasopressor therapy.
